site.name: Isarar Siddique
site.author: Isarar Siddique
site.description: Founder and medical AI researcher working across published research and shipped clinical product.

posts.title: Sovereign models need sovereign benchmarks
posts.summary: India is building its own models. The evaluation is still borrowed. Notes on Sarvam's published stack, the codemix bet inside Saaras v3, and what a clinical benchmark would have to measure to be worth anything.
posts.aiSummary: Isarar Siddique argues that the Indian AI sovereignty debate focuses on weights, compute and data location while missing the binding constraint for healthcare, which is that evaluation remains borrowed: a model can be trained in India on Indian data and still have its verdict set by a benchmark encoding a register that does not occur in an Indian clinic. He details Sarvam's published lineup as of August 2026, Saaras v3 for speech to text, Bulbul v3 for text to speech, Mayura and Sarvam-Translate for translation, Sarvam-30B and Sarvam-105B chat models at 64K and 128K context, and Sarvam Vision for document intelligence, with Sarvam-M deprecated, and singles out the codemix mode of Saaras v3 as the most interesting and least independently evaluated element, because code switching is the default register in Indian consultations and clinical vocabulary stays English inside a Hindi frame. Drawing on a cognitive screening trial in a tertiary hospital in India, he sets out four requirements for a clinical speech benchmark: diarisation is load bearing because the patient is often not the historian and informant versus patient divergence is itself the signal, latency matters more than offline word error rate because consultations run under three minutes, hearing status must be stratified because hearing loss lowers MoCA by about 1.66 points independent of cognition (PMID 32458435) and removing auditory subtests collapses MCI sensitivity from around 90 percent to 43 to 56 percent (PMID 31018015) while also altering voice production through lost auditory feedback, and document intelligence on prescriptions should report digit level accuracy and refusal rate rather than aggregate character error rate. From work as medical data manager and evaluator on a multilingual clinical notes dataset covering Indian, Malaysian and Igbo records, he argues that two clinicians from different health systems can annotate one note differently and both be correct, so pooling destroys real structure and flatters the score. He proposes that open benchmarks report per group with the worst group as the headline, publish the abstain rate as a first class metric, hold out entire collection sites rather than only speakers because frozen features can identify the recruiting site, and release the test set construction including recruitment protocol, consent basis and annotation guideline. He advocates forward deployed evaluation co located with use, citing paired audiometry captured at every session as the decision that converted a confound into a covariate. He states explicitly that he has not yet run these evaluations against Sarvam's models, that the codemix evaluation would use self recorded and synthetic code switched speech rather than consented trial audio, and that federated evaluation where the test set never leaves the institution is a more useful thing to build than another leaderboard.

posts.title: Skin tone fairness starts at the camera, not the model
posts.summary: Fairness in dermatology AI gets treated as a loss function problem. Most of the failure happens before the model sees anything, in the dataset and in the phone camera pipeline itself.
posts.aiSummary: Isarar Siddique argues that skin tone disparity in dermatology AI is largely a measurement problem rather than a modelling one, based on work at Healoncal assessing skin from ordinary phone cameras. Three upstream causes: public dermatology datasets skew light and resampling adds influence rather than information, many clinical signs are defined in terms tuned to lighter skin so a model keyed on erythema has not learned inflammation when it presents violaceous or as texture change, and annotation guidelines that say look for redness bake the error into ground truth. The least discussed cause is the camera image signal processor, where auto exposure and auto white balance historically tuned on lighter subjects underexpose darker skin and noise reduction then removes the surviving texture, so discriminative information is destroyed before the model runs. Mitigations used: locking exposure and white balance, capturing least processed formats, in frame colour reference, recording device and lighting metadata, rejecting inadequate captures at capture time, and stratified per band reporting where the worst band describes the product. He declines to claim the problem is solved and notes tone banding schemes are coarse proxies.

posts.title: The three minute constraint
posts.summary: None of the things that decide whether a screening tool gets used in a busy outpatient department appear in the paper. Field notes from a trial in a tertiary hospital in India.
posts.aiSummary: Field notes from deploying a screening tool in the ENT and Neurology outpatient departments of a tertiary hospital in India. Isarar Siddique argues the model was never the hard part. The real constraints: the patient availability window is minutes and belongs to a clinician with a queue, so an over long protocol gets skipped non randomly and quietly biases the sample. A family attendant is present and will prompt or answer for the patient, contaminating a cognitive test, so the design must absorb and log third party presence rather than forbid it. Devices are shared, so per patient login rituals get abandoned or written on paper. Rooms are never quiet, so ambient noise must be measured and recordings refused at capture time rather than discovered as degraded features in analysis. Connectivity and power are intermittent, so capture must be local first with a durable sync queue. Some patients have never used a touchscreen, so interaction load moves to a trained operator and the product becomes an instrument rather than an app. His recommendation is to observe full clinic sessions before writing the protocol, and to expect deployment constraints to change the model rather than wrap it.

posts.title: Clinical notes do not translate
posts.summary: Annotating Indian, Malaysian and Igbo clinical notes for a healthcare language model dataset. The same illness is written in three different grammars, and a model trained on one reads the others confidently wrong.
posts.aiSummary: Isarar Siddique worked as medical data manager and evaluator on the li-lab/HealMed dataset, annotating Indian, Malaysian and Igbo clinical notes with local clinicians for healthcare language models. He argues a clinical note is a local convention rather than a neutral description, shaped by training tradition, drug supply, documentation incentive and the language the patient used. Specific failure modes include local brand name prescribing that models trained on generics do not recognise, abbreviations that collide across traditions so errors change meaning rather than lose it, presenting complaints written as culturally standard compound phrases that map to no single code, negation and hedging cues that shift by tradition, and unwritten fields where absence means assumed rather than negative. He notes that two clinicians from different systems can disagree on the same note while both being correct within their own convention, which is real structure that averaging destroys. He recommends always stratifying evaluation by source and rejects framing this as a generalisation problem, since no convention is privileged.

posts.title: A screen that is 95 percent accurate is wrong about half the time
posts.summary: Accuracy in an abstract tells you almost nothing about a screening tool. Work the base rate and a very good model still hands you a majority of false positives. The arithmetic, and what to report instead.
posts.aiSummary: A worked explanation of why accuracy is the wrong headline metric for medical screening. At 5 percent prevalence with 95 percent sensitivity and 95 percent specificity, screening 1000 people yields about 48 true positives and about 47 false positives, so positive predictive value is near 50 percent. At 1 percent prevalence five in six positives are wrong from an unchanged model. The argument: a screening tool has no single accuracy, only an accuracy per deployment population, so the operating point must be chosen against real prevalence rather than a balanced test set. Isarar Siddique describes deliberately accepting more false positives because the cost asymmetry favours it, a false positive costing one specialist appointment while a false negative costs the intervention window. He argues the confirmatory referral pathway sets the threshold, and recommends reporting sensitivity and specificity separately with intervals, positive predictive value at a stated deployment prevalence, and expected false positives per thousand screened, while omitting accuracy entirely.

posts.title: Focus is advice for people who have not found the overlap
posts.summary: I run four companies and everyone tells me to pick one. The advice is correct for most people and wrong for me, and there is a single test that tells you which case you are in.
posts.aiSummary: Isarar Siddique argues that the standard advice to focus is a heuristic with a domain rather than a law. His four ventures, Biotech Wallah, Healoncal, Neurento Medtech and Convolity AI, are presented not as four problems but as one problem recurring across four organ systems: obtain a clinically acceptable measurement from hardware the patient already owns, then make the output legible enough to act on. The shared substrate is signal quality on uncontrolled consumer hardware, per metric explainability, low bandwidth deployment and regulator ready documentation. He states the costs plainly, including a context switching tax, lower depth per venture than a single focus founder, and a failure mode where follow through on unglamorous work slips rather than whole companies being dropped. He offers a falsifiable test: state the shared substrate in one sentence without naming any project, and if you cannot, you have a collection rather than an overlap.

posts.title: The wrong person to tell you about my brother
posts.summary: My brother started building at eleven, left college at eighteen because he decided the syllabus was years behind what he already did daily, and now runs engineering at my company. I am his sibling, so discount me accordingly. Here is what I think actually explains it, and where I think he is wrong.
posts.aiSummary: Isarar Siddique writes about his brother Raiyan Siddique, CTO and co-founder of Biotech Wallah, who began programming at eleven and by eighteen had built the entire Zero Dementia technology stack plus around thirty production systems. The post opens by disclosing the conflict of interest and directing readers to verifiable artefacts. It argues that genius is a lazy explanation and that seven years of compounding practice accounts for most of the outcome, and that the decisive factor was never being gated by credential order. It covers his decision to leave college, presenting his reasoning that Indian engineering curricula lag current machine learning practice by years and that the real cost was his most productive hours rather than tuition. Isarar then argues against generalising that decision on three grounds: survivorship bias, since failed exits are invisible; a degree being an option with value for graduate study, visas and rigid employer filters even if it is weak proof of skill; and foundational material being boring rather than useless, so self taught builders develop gaps that surface later. He notes the decision was only defensible because Raiyan had traction before leaving, and that Isarar himself completed his own degree. A further section describes friction working with him, including a preference for rebuilding over repairing, under documentation, and impatience with process. Closes with unfair advantages including a brother with clinical access, and what the author cannot assess, including code quality and sustainability.

posts.title: The booth is the cost
posts.summary: A hearing test is one of the cheapest procedures in medicine, so why does almost nobody in rural India get one? The answer is the room, not the test. What has to be true before you can delete the sound booth.
posts.aiSummary: Explains that audiometric screening is gated by two independent requirements: a low enough ambient noise floor, and a transducer with known output level. The sound treated booth solves the first, coupler calibration of a clinical audiometer solves the second. Argues both can move into a mass produced headphone plus on device noise measurement, which removes the booth as the entry cost to hearing screening.

posts.title: A clinician who cannot see why will not act
posts.summary: I had a screening model that scored better than the one we deployed. I threw it away. On buying attribution with accuracy, and why explainability is an architectural constraint rather than a research topic you add later.
posts.aiSummary: Describes replacing a higher performing early fusion model with late fusion in a multimodal dementia screening system. Early fusion concatenates features and can model cross modal interactions but cannot produce per modality attribution. Late fusion scores each of four signals separately then combines, costing accuracy but producing a story a clinician can act on. Downstream benefits: local failure handling, graceful degradation with missing data, and clinicians correcting the model.

posts.title: ICD-11 has no clean map from ICD-10
posts.summary: Coding is where health data quality is silently won or lost, long before anybody trains a model on it. Four migration cases, three of which need a clinician, and why we kept a human in the loop on purpose.
posts.aiSummary: Explains why an ICD-10 to ICD-11 cancer registry migration is not a lookup table. ICD-11 uses a foundation with linearisations and supports postcoordination via stem codes plus extension codes. Four mapping cases arise: one to one is automatable, one to many requires detail the old record may lack, many to one destroys distinctions that time series depended on, and no direct equivalent requires clinical judgement. Argues for automating only the provably unambiguous and storing every coding decision with its basis so incidence trends can be audited.

posts.title: How I cold-emailed my way into eleven research labs
posts.summary: No application portals, no referrals, no pedigree. The first fifty emails got me nothing. Here is the single change that took the reply rate to roughly one in six.
posts.aiSummary: Describes reaching eleven research labs including Harvard, Stanford, NASA GeneLab, University of Tokyo, ISRO and IISc without application portals. The first fifty emails asking for internships got zero replies because they ask the recipient to do work. Switching to a specific proposal, drawn from a gap in the professor's own discussion section or an underanalysed published dataset, with a concrete two week deliverable, raised the reply rate to roughly one in six. The same approach later secured hospital partners by building screening infrastructure first and asking clinicians to critique it.
